item.title: I pitted my paid VPN against free options, and my subscription doesn't feel worth it anymore
item.itunes:title: I pitted my paid VPN against free options, and my subscription doesn't feel worth it anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have had a Surfshark subscription for nearly 5 years now, and it's been a good deal, all things considered. It costs me around $2.5 a month, and has helped ensure traffic privacy and avoid geo-blocking and ISP throttling (for the most part). During this time, there were periods where I dabbled in free VPN services like Proton VPN and Opera browser's built-in VPN.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Free VPN has restrictions and, often, sketchy behavior, but I wanted to check if it can replace a paid service for the right user. So, I decided to test my Surfshark subscription against Proton VPN, Windscribe, and Opera's built-in VPN. I tested everything on Ethernet to eliminate Wi-Fi variables, and used Cloudflare Speed Test and Fast.com to test the percentage drop in speeds.

Since speed is just one aspect of a VPN, I also compared the four services on data caps, device limits, the choice of servers, security features, and privacy policies.

I stopped using free VPNs after I learned what they do with your traffic

That free VPN is probably selling something and it might be you

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Speed and browsing experience

Surfshark proved its worth, but free VPNs weren't far behind

I have a 200 Mbps plan, and it mostly shows up as 190 Mbps in speed tests. I started my testing with Surfshark, followed by Opera, Proton VPN, and Windscribe. For each VPN, I tested the "best," "fastest," or "optimal" server shown by the app, followed by the closest server and also a long-haul connection. Since I'm testing in India, this helped me simulate a representative test for a wider audience. I also ran three runs of speed tests on both Cloudflare and Fast.com, measuring the median speed.

Expectedly, Surfshark showed almost no drop in speeds on the fastest server (Singapore). YouTube performance at 1440p as well as 4K was nearly instantaneous. I changed the server to the Netherlands, as that's usually the one most VPN apps default to when choosing the best server, and it also served as a longer connection geographically. Speed and latency worsened slightly, but the browsing experience remained essentially the same.

While Fast.com uses Netflix's CDNs to give an idea of your connection's streaming performance, Cloudflare's speed test is a more general indicator of how it would behave across the internet. The Fast.com numbers were almost always higher than those of Cloudflare, so I noted the percentage drop for both tests at the end.

Moving to Opera's built-in VPN, I picked the "Optimal" server shown by the browser, which turned out to be the least optimal of all. It delivered a few hundred Kbps in speeds, so I abandoned it and manually selected the Asia region. Compared to Surfshark, Opera dropped the speed significantly, so I switched to the Europe server and tested again. It was only marginally faster.

YouTube still ran well, even at 1440p, with only a second or two of buffering time when skipping ahead. However, on Opera's Asia server, YouTube simply refused to load (it worked fine on Europe). I guess YouTube's VPN blocking policy caught the Asia server but not Europe. That said, other video sites like Dailymotion and TikTok worked without problems on the Asia server.

Switching gears from built-in browser VPN to the wildly popular Proton VPN, it took me a while to find the free sign-up option on its account creation page. Proton VPN doesn't allow you to manually choose a server; it auto-selects from a list of 10 free servers. However, you can use the "Change server" option to shuffle to a different server if you aren't satisfied with the performance.

Proton's performance was way more impressive than that of Opera's built-in VPN. It retained over half of my connection's maximum speed, and the results stayed mostly similar across its best server (Romania), the Netherlands, and Canada.

Lastly, I tested Windscribe, another free and popular VPN app. It allows sign-up without providing an email, so that's what I chose. Giving your email address has benefits, but I'd get to that in the next section. The best server on Windscribe was Hong Kong during my testing, but Fast.com showed an abnormal 240 Kbps result. I ran Cloudflare's test and got over 100 Mbps, so I searched about it.

It turns out Netflix throttles known VPN servers, which shows up as a poor speed test on Fast.com. Cloudflare's test, on the other hand, shows the actual speed of the VPN tunnel. I changed the server to the Netherlands, and sure enough, Fast.com showed a proper result. Windscribe retained a significant amount of my network speed, just like Proton VPN. YouTube, Dailymotion, and other sites worked perfectly, too.

To rank each VPN based on performance, I compared the best-case scenarios for each app. I calculated the percentage drop for Fast.com and Cloudflare separately.

Data caps and device limits

This is where the cracks start to show

Speed is one of the most important parameters of a VPN, but it's not the only one. Free VPNs need to restrict usage in one way or the other, and data caps and device limits are a few ways to do that. Surfshark allows unlimited simultaneous connections with no data caps, just like many paid services.

Starting with the worst performer in the speed section, Opera's built-in VPN works only in the browser (desktop and mobile both), so the rest of the device stays out of coverage. That said, there's no data cap or device limit, so you can continue using it on every device without worrying about exhausting your usage. Considering the speeds aren't that great, the question is how much you'll be able to use it anyway.

Proton VPN doesn't have any data cap, but you can only use it on one active connection. It uses your email address for the account sign-up, and you can have it installed on multiple devices, but only use it on one device at a time.

Windscribe doesn't limit the number of simultaneous connections, but it's the only app on the list with a data cap, limiting you to 2GB of monthly usage (which I exhausted during the testing itself). You can increase that to 10GB if you provide your email address, but even that's too low for a whole month. I checked my browser's data usage on Windows, and saw just under 50GB of usage in the last 30 days.

Firefox's built-in browser VPN provides users with 50GB of free monthly usage (currently unlimited till Jan 31, 2027), but I couldn't test it here in India.

Winner: Surfshark, followed by Proton VPN

Server choice and feature set

Flexibility and security

Many users look to a VPN to access geo-blocked content on streaming services, and a limited choice of servers hurts that proposition. This factor isn't as important as speed and data caps, but it's still important. Maintaining servers requires money, so free VPNs will obviously limit your choice, but different services do it to a different extent.

While Surfshark provides servers across 100 countries, Proton VPN has a small list of 10 free countries, which you can shuffle around. The list includes popular locations, such as the United States, Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, and more, but it's still a small list. Windscribe has a similar list of 10 free countries, but you can manually choose the location. That said, the 10GB monthly limit makes streaming a non-starter.

Opera browser is even more restrictive, as it only offers three regions: Americas, Europe, and Asia, so you can't choose a specific country.

In terms of features, Proton VPN, Windscribe, and Opera offer a kill switch feature, which automatically blocks the internet connection to prevent IP address leaks, in case your VPN drops unexpectedly. Note that Opera's browser VPN is limited to the, well, browser. P2P traffic is not supported on either of them on the free tiers, but Opera and Windscribe offer basic blocking for ads and trackers. Surfshark obviously includes all routing, traffic, and browsing features you expect from a paid VPN.

Winner: Surfshark, followed by Proton VPN

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Privacy and no-logs policy

Some free VPNs are better than others

Finally, we come to perhaps the most important parameter of all. The whole point of moving your traffic through a VPN tunnel is to protect it from prying eyes. If your VPN service itself is untrustworthy, you might as well not use one at all. While it's already known that using a VPN doesn't hide everything you do on the internet, it still helps to know the privacy policies of every service when choosing one.

Surfshark has a strict no-logs policy with RAM-only servers that wipe all data on reboot. It is audited by Deloitte and Cure53, and it's based in the Netherlands, which is part of the Nine Eyes alliance. Surfshark's RAM-only servers and user data deletion within 15 minutes of disconnection mitigate jurisdiction risks. Surfshark is also bound by GDPR rules, giving users strict rights over personal data.

Proton VPN and Windscribe are also audited by entities like Securitum, Packetlabs, and Leviathan Security Group. Proton is based in Switzerland, while Windscribe is under Norwegian jurisdiction. Windscribe is known to run RAM-only (diskless) servers, whereas Proton VPN uses full-disk encryption (LUKS) instead.

Proton VPN requires an email address, but has a better no-logs policy, since Windscribe needs to store your last timestamp and 30-day data usage for free accounts. Also, Proton is protected by Swiss law, where VPNs aren't required to retain metadata, but Windscribe's proof of no-logs relies on real-world server seizures and court dismissals instead.

Opera's browser VPN is bound by GDPR rules, since it's based in Norway. It doesn't store our browsing activity, DNS queries, or originating IP addresses, but the browser collects other device identifiers and usage data.

Winner: Proton VPN, but it's not that simple — Proton VPN has open-source apps and the strongest legal protection. Surfshark wins on RAM-only servers and Big Four audits, but has jurisdiction trade-offs. Windscribe has RAM-only servers and real-world proof, but stores last-seen date and is headquartered in Canada.

I can realistically move to Proton VPN

Free VPN doesn't have to be unusable

Surfshark has served me well, but I'm starting to feel that I'm not really making the most of my subscription. I don't use more than one device at a time, and I rarely try to access geo-blocked content. Besides, all the secondary features part of my subscription don't matter to me all that much. Surfshark is one of the most affordable VPNs on the market, but Proton VPN ticks a lot of boxes as a free service.

For starters, the speed difference between Proton and Surfshark isn't huge. The real-world browsing experience is indistinguishable. Then, there's the limited server choice, but if I'm not looking for a specific location, that's not a big problem. Proton's privacy policy is also the strictest of the bunch, and its free tier enjoys the same security protections as the paid one. There's no data cap and the single connection limit is less harsh than it sounds in practice.

Proton VPN uses revenue from paid subscriptions to maintain a decent level of service for free members. The next time my Surfshark subscription comes up for renewal, I'll gladly skip the 2-year $50 fee and move to Proton VPN permanently.

5 open-source apps that are so good their premium versions are worth paying for

Not paywalled, just worth paying for.

32
By  Yash Patel

Paid vs. free VPN can be a close call

Although most free VPNs are guilty of selling user data or making other big compromises, not all of them operate this way. Proton VPN is one of the best options out there, and you can realistically use the free tier for years. I've enjoyed Surfshark for almost five years, but Proton VPN's free offering has made me reconsider my subscription.

Privacy and no-logs policy

Finally, we come to perhaps the most important parameter of all. The whole point of moving your traffic through a VPN tunnel is to protect it from prying eyes. Proton's privacy policy is also the strictest of the bunch, and its free tier enjoys the same security protections as the paid one. There's no data cap and the single connection limit is less harsh than it sounds in practice.

Proton VPN uses revenue from paid subscriptions to maintain a decent level of service for free members. The next time my Surfshark subscription comes up for renewal, I'll gladly skip the 2-year $50 fee and move to Proton VPN permanently.

Although most free VPNs are guilty of selling user data or making other big compromises, not all of them operate this way. item.itunes:summary:
My adventures of building a smart home on a shoestring budget are taking an interesting turn. It turns out that I don’t need to splurge on costly smart home devices. Thanks to my colleague Adam Conway’s first-hand experience of building cheap smart home sensors with ESP32, my smart home dreams got a serious boost.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So, I went on a sensor shopping spree and ended up buying more than a handful of them. I ensured that I could pair them with my ESP32 board and eventually integrate them into Home Assistant. Despite the learning curve (and a few weekends), it was totally worth it. If you don’t mind tinkering, here are seven sensors under $10 that have been absolute game-changers for my smart home.

Electromechanical sensor for doors and windows

A simple and reliable way for security automation

For security reasons and basic automation, I picked up an electromechanical sensor, better known as a magnetic reed switch. While starting small, it was surprisingly easy to plug into an ESPHome board, define it in the YAML file, and flash it. Dealing with the filters was also interesting, since I could set up an automation to alert me if the door was left open or if someone opened it after midnight.

Once I fine-tuned the filters, I added some basic automation to trigger only when I am not home. Since this sensor doesn’t depend on a battery or an internet connection, it is fast, reliable, and continues to work even if the network is down. Hence, I installed a couple of them on my home’s back door and windows.

Temperature and humidity sensor for weather reports

Helps in planning the day and other chores

I was amazed at how the temperature and humidity sensor had quickly become a household favorite. Using the data derived from it, my family checks the weather card before stepping out for errands or meetups.

Getting its report data took some tinkering, but now it pipes those details into Home Assistant. I also combine it with Pirate Weather for more precise local forecasts. It has helped me choose comfortable clothing more than once.

Next, I feed this sensor’s data into a locally hosted LLM to get better clothing recommendations. Additionally, I hope that it will help me plan room renovations and prevent mold.

Motion sensor for presence detection

Commandeer automations and alerts based on your presence

I use my phone’s location for presence detection, but the delay would bug me. So I grabbed a Passive Infrared (PIR) to fix that and also some automation that involves motion detection. While the sensor’s setup was straightforward, it initially went wrong. I powered it from a 3.3V pin instead of the 5V pin. After correcting that, it didn’t take me long to get it working with ESPHome firmware.

Now it helps me run some presence-based automations and also alerts me whenever stray dogs sneak into our garden. Next, I plan to group it with presence sensors that use only Bluetooth.

Light Dependent Resistor for smart lighting

Adjusting the automated lights more precisely

Time-based automations are no-brainers, but sunset and sunrise don’t happen at those fixed hours. That’s why I thought a Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) sensor could help me. With that, I adjusted my automation to control the indoor lighting based on the brightness outside dynamically. The transitions now feel more natural, and not jarring or sudden.

For fun, I even use the same brightness data to experiment with my camera’s exposure triangle — aperture, ISO, and shutter speed, when taking a few pictures. That’s my bonus for using such an inexpensive sensor.

Sound detection sensors to trigger alerts

Staying aware of abnormal events and improving security

A simple sound detection sensor makes my washing machine smart. It picks up the hums or rattles when the machine is in use, and the Home Assistant notifies me when the laundry cycle is complete. But that often misfires when neighbors blast music. I combine it with the PIR sensor to create a DIY security system that listens and detects, especially at night.

The primary challenge is the issue of false positives. Besides a little calibration to help it distinguish between neighbors’ repairs and laundry time, it’s been incredibly helpful.

Water Level Sensor for storage tanks

One step to avoid water wastage or flooding

I spent several hours getting this to work, but it paid off. The water level depth sensor helps me monitor the tank levels and alerts me to shut off the pump before it overflows through Home Assistant. I’m still looking for a suitable smart plug to automate turning off the pump.

Since I live in a flood-prone area, I am also using this sensor to track the water accumulation just outside my home. While it works most effectively during heavy rains, it helps prepare for more severe monsoons. Meanwhile, I get to save gallons of water by preventing tanks from overflowing.

Soil hygrometer sensor for garden

Taking care of the plants with data

Gardening has always been a challenge for my family. My mom’s the only enthusiastic one, but she struggles sometimes. To help her, I added a soil hygrometer sensor on our plant beds. It measures soil moisture and reports so that we know how much water the plants need. Hopefully, it helps my family understand that overwatering doesn’t help. After all, we too want to understand the plants’ needs better.

The biggest challenge so far has been to keep the sensor functioning and protect it from accidental splashes. So far, I’ve been using makeshift wrappers to keep the sensor dry till I get a better enclosure.

Building a smart home doesn’t have to be expensive

It’s difficult to describe how satisfying these cheap little sensors work together to make my smart home shine. The only challenge is to get a proper enclosure to protect them from dust and weather. I’m exploring some 3D printing options and hoping to pick up some design wisdom from my colleague, Jeff Butts, to create custom cases. That would be worth checking to ensure these sub-$10 sensors keep my smart home connected.

item.itunes:title: I replaced Spotify's bloated desktop app with a native open-source client, and it plays my local files too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent enough time with Spotify's desktop app to know exactly what I want from it—play my music, get out of the way, and stop making me feel like I'm running a web browser just to listen to a playlist.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, Spotify's official client has accumulated enough baggage over the years that I started looking elsewhere. I wasn't looking for another bloated wrapper pretending to be a native app. I wanted something that actually felt like software built for my PC.

That's what led me to Spotifast. It's an open-source Spotify client that takes a surprisingly different approach to the desktop experience, and after using it for a while, I started wondering why I hadn't switched sooner. But the biggest surprise wasn't how it handled Spotify itself.

Spotify doesn't need to be this heavy

A native client shouldn't feel like a web app

The Spotify desktop app feels oddly overqualified for the job. I want to search, hit play, manage a queue, and move on. Instead, it feels like a website living in its own window. For something whose job is playing music, that has seemed backwards to me for the longest time.

Spotifast takes a different route altogether. It is built in Rust with egui and fastframe, rather than wrapping Spotify's web experience inside a browser engine. The difference is immediately noticeable, and very welcome, too. Spotifast's interface feels snappy and starts up near-instantly; the project claims memory usage of roughly 100-250mb. Spotify, on the other hand, consumes between 600 and 700 MB of RAM while it's open and playing music.

There is one catch, however. Spotifast requires Spotify Premium for playback. Free accounts can browse and search, but they can't use Spotifast as a player. Setting it up requires registering a Spotify app and authenticating, which takes a little more effort than downloading the Spotify app from the Windows Store. That is extra friction, but it is upfront.

Once that's done, I get the Spotify library I use without a miniature browser on my desktop. But the fun didn't stop after installing a new, lighter Spotify client. Things got considerably better once Spotifast began behaving like the music player I remember enjoying, and now it's an app I spend a lot of time on, daily.

3 Jellyfin clients that finally make it look as good as Plex and Spotify

Make the interface of your media clients better for what you actually use them for

10
By  Ty Sherback

Spotifast has brought back the desktop music player for me

Spotify forgot that people like making things their own

Even though I downloaded Spotifast with the sole intent of having a lighter, different Spotify experience, I was genuinely taken aback by how much it feels like an old-school desktop music player. I can change its appearance with themes, and it goes far beyond a handful of dark-mode variations.

In "the big 2026," Spotifast still supports Windows Media Player's .WMZ skins, and even Winamp skins. It's about as gloriously unnecessarily as it sounds, and that's exactly why I love it.

My favorite feature, though, is Spotifast's MilkDrop integration. It supports more than 10,000 visualizer presets, which have turned my Spotify playlist into something that can actually occupy the screen instead of leaving me staring at the album artwork. Plus, these visualizations work with the lyrics, too, so it's not like I'm trading lyrics for the visualizations. After not thinking about MilkDrop in years, going through hundreds of visualizations on my new local music player felt like I'd been transported back to the 2000s.

The rest of the interface follows the same philosophy. There is proper queue management, lyrics, media-key support, system-tray controls, and the ability to control playback on other devices through Spotify Connect. Google Cast and Sonos support are there too, so this isn't merely a local replacement for Spotify's player.

Throughout my time using Spotifast, none of the features felt bolted on as afterthoughts. The player, library, queue, visualizers, and customization all exist within the same native application, and the app itself feels thoughtfully designed around them. Spotifast seems to care that I actually own a PC and might want to personalize what runs on it.

Then I discovered I could put my own music in it

My Spotify library and local collection finally live together

The feature that actually made Spotifast stick on my PC was local-file playback. I have accumulated enough music over the years that Spotify will never contain everything I want to listen to, which usually means keeping a second player around for the stuff that isn't in its catalog. Spotifast makes that separation rather pointless.

I've been holding on to an MP3 folder of my favorite songs ever since I got my first music player back in 2005. Despite spending double-digit hours on my PC every day for the past decade, I refuse to spend a minute manually adding each song to my Spotify playlists one by one. As such, I may not have listened to a single song in one of the five hundred songs I've been carrying, but seeing them populate on my PC's default music player, right alongside my Spotify playlists, was certainly an experience.

Yes, Spotify itself supports local files, but that misses why I care about them here. Spotifast is designed as a desktop music player rather than a window into Spotify's service, so my own collection doesn't feel like a secondary feature buried in the settings. It fits the entire experience.

That is ultimately what changed my mind about this being merely a lighter Spotify client. I started using it because I wanted something less cumbersome, but I kept it because it behaves like the desktop music player I wanted Spotify to be. And somehow, it also swallowed the job of my local player.

I gave Jellyfin a Kodi makeover, and my media library felt brand-new

My media center has never looked better

2
By  Samarveer Singh

I didn't realize how much I missed owning my music player

The funny thing is, I wasn't trying to replace Spotify. I just wanted the desktop experience to stop feeling obligatory. After years of using apps, it was refreshing to use something that treats the PC as a platform worth using, rather than as a place to park a web interface.

I still use Spotify because its catalog is hard to beat, but I no longer feel like I have to accept everything that comes with its official client. If an open-source project can make a music player feel this personal, the bar for companies building them should be much higher.

Spotifast

item.itunes:title: I skipped buying an expensive NAS, and turned my old gaming PC into a media server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently got a new PC to replace my old HP Omen gaming PC. I've been thinking about getting a multi-bay NAS for media storage, but I'm also on a tight budget. I was thinking of ways to repurpose the computer. The two ideas came together. Since a NAS is a computer-driven storage device, I figured I might as well add as much storage as I can and use it to store and serve my media.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My gaming rig still has more horsepower than a typical home NAS. I wanted to run Jellyfin and Emby on separate ports. I also needed my Nvidia Shield Pro's Plex server to have access to the files on its storage drives. Doing so would let it act as a DIY NAS and media server at the same time.

Cleaning up and sticking with Windows

It accomplishes my goals

The Omen runs Windows 11 Pro. Enthusiasts will ask why I didn't install OpenMediaVault (OMV) or TrueNAS. I have already turned an old Windows Home Server into a dumb NAS with OpenMediaVault. However, my old gaming rig is a temporary media server until I can afford a proper NAS. After that, I'll use the old gaming rig for something else. I'm also connecting external drives to it for additional storage, which isn't ideal for OMV's SMART health monitoring support.

It accomplishes what I want, and I have a backup PC in case my new ABS machine goes out at some point. I can also use it for other smaller side projects while it continues to serve media. I didn't reformat and reinstall. I cleaned up space on the drives, and it gave me the chance to do some overlooked maintenance, like updating the local drives' firmware and installing a long-overdue BIOS update.

How to turn an old PC into a NAS

If you have an old PC still lying around, you could turn it into a NAS.

9
By  Adam Conway

Choosing a media server platform

I don't have to pick just one

A benefit of turning a PC into a media server is not having to commit to just one platform. I installed Plex, Emby, and Jellyfin and ran each of them on a different port. I also plan on installing Navidrome to see what it can do with my ripped CD library. That lets me get familiar with each media server platform and decide which one I will stick with.

Each one has its pros and cons, and I can move between them to fill the feature gaps I may want for my media. My old gaming rig includes an Intel i7 8700, 32GB DDR4 RAM, and a GeForce GTX 1060 3GB graphics card, which is considered legacy for gaming. But it is still plenty for transcoding tasks and running the media server software. I have been able to access my library reliably on all screens. Even my CD library remotely with Jellybox.

Transcoding is the part everyone gets wrong, and the fix is usually a cheaper GPU than you think

You don't have to rebuild your entire server

By  Samarveer Singh

Where the PC falls short of a NAS

Adding a ton of storage is an issue

Somehow, I've been getting by with a paltry 500GB Samsung M.2 NVMe drive I installed when I initially got the machine. There's also a 1 TB SATA drive for storage. That is plenty of room for media servers and their cache, plus other light software for small computer tasks. For storage, I connected a hodgepodge of different external drives of various sizes with my ripped media. The good thing about the old HP Omen is that it has plenty of USB 3.0 ports to connect multiple drives.

However, I still yearn for a proper 4-bay NAS so I can fill it with 16TB or 20TB drives. I thought of getting a 16TB external drive, or a larger SATA drive, but storage isn't cheap. A WD 16TB external drive is nearly the same cost as a bare NAS, so I will keep getting by with what I have. Also, I can do more with my PC while streaming my media throughout my house.

Two-bay NAS boxes are the worst way to start self-hosting, and a used mini PC is better for home server projects

A used mini PC makes a better self-hosting server than a 2-bay NAS

3
By  Ayush Pande

Accessing gaming PC storage on my Shield TV Pro

I mounted it like a NAS

Having a choice of server platforms made me realize I prefer to run Plex on my Nvidia Shield TV Pro. But since I moved the external drives connected to the Shield to my old gaming rig, I mounted them like a real NAS appliance. That also lets me clean up a mess of drives, cables, and hubs under my TV.

I created a media share on my PC and mounted it on the Shield TV Pro through its network storage section. Once it was connected, I could play all the DVD, CD, and Blu-ray rips from my drive. The HP is connected to my network via Ethernet, and files seemed to play fine since all connectivity is Gigabit. The only times I had an issue were when using Plex on Wi-Fi devices, which is always a performance bottleneck.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

An old gaming PC can earn a place as a repurposed media server

Gaming rigs are generally packed with powerful hardware to run for years and are upgradable. So, even when they lose their edge, they are well suited to be repurposed for other tasks. Using mine for storage and as a media server has been working well. However, keeping it powered on 24/7 isn't helping with electricity costs. For now, it works to consolidate all my media on one storage appliance.

item.title: I finally found a better way to search, organize, and manage files on Windows
item.itunes:title: I finally found a better way to search, organize, and manage files on Windows
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Managing files on Windows shouldn't mean opening endless folders or remembering where everything is saved. I've tried different ways to keep my documents, downloads, and project resources organized, but finding a system that works across different file types isn't always easy.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's what made me take a closer look at TagSpaces. After spending some time with it, I realized that keeping my documents and project resources in order didn't have to involve so much manual sorting.

What is TagSpaces?

A local-first file manager with more ways to organize information

TagSpaces is an open-source, cross-platform file manager for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It combines file browsing, tagging, search, and built-in file previews in one application. It also includes basic editors for creating and editing Markdown, HTML, and plain-text files. The tool works with files on your local storage without requiring an account or a central database.

After installing TagSpaces, I found its interface fairly easy to navigate. It supports local folders as well as S3-compatible storage, so I can access files in different locations without changing my existing setup. Rather than introducing another complicated system, TagSpaces adds an organizational layer to the files already on my computer.

I stopped relying on folders alone to organize my files

TagSpaces makes file organization feel different

Traditional file organization depends heavily on folder names and subfolders. TagSpaces lets me categorize files by attaching multiple color-coded tags to the same item. For example, a project document can carry labels such as work, research, and 2026 without creating separate copies in different directories. That means I can find the same document through multiple categories without duplicating it.

Creating tags is straightforward. TagSpaces lets me define custom labels and group them by projects, file types, or other categories. I can also apply tags to multiple selected files, which saves time when organizing a larger collection. I can also choose how TagSpaces stores this information. Depending on the selected tagging method, it can add tags directly to filenames or save them in separate JSON sidecar files inside hidden .ts folders. The latter is useful when I want to preserve original filenames.

This free self-hosted file explorer links all of my storage into one web-based UI

I set up a self-hosted file manager that lets me browse local drives, cloud storage, and network shares, all from one clean web interface.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Finding and browsing files is much easier now

Search beyond filenames and get a better view of your files

Searching through a large collection of files is usually where things get frustrating. TagSpaces gives me more ways to narrow down results than simply remembering a filename. Its search considers filenames, descriptions, folder paths, and assigned tags. It can also search inside supported file contents when full-text indexing is enabled. Plain-text formats such as TXT, Markdown, HTML, and source code files are supported in the free Lite edition, while searching inside supported PDF and Office documents requires Pro.

Search filters provide another level of control. I can narrow results by file type, size, creation date, or last-modified date. Its tag search supports AND, OR, and NOT logic. I can require files to have all selected tags, find files with at least one of several tags, or exclude specific tags from the results. This comes in handy when I'm searching for documents associated with specific projects.

For browsing, TagSpaces offers grid and list perspectives, while additional options such as Gallery are available in Pro. The grid layout is useful for scanning mixed collections, whereas a gallery-style view works particularly well for visual content. It also generates thumbnails for supported file formats and includes built-in viewers for images, PDFs, videos, ebooks, and other file types. These previews make it easier to identify files without opening them individually.

Not competing with advanced file managers

A useful companion, not a complete replacement

TagSpaces isn't designed to replace every file manager on Windows, and that's its biggest strength. Tools such as Directory Opus and FreeCommander are better suited to users who need advanced file operations, dual-pane navigation, batch processing, and extensive customization. TagSpaces takes a more organizational approach.

During my testing, I found it particularly useful for tracking research documents, reference material, and resources spread across multiple projects. It doesn't offer the same level of control over file operations as dedicated power-user tools, and setting up tags takes some initial effort, especially when dealing with a large collection.

File Explorer is still perfectly capable of handling routine tasks, while advanced alternatives offer more control over complex file operations. I see TagSpaces fitting alongside these tools, particularly when I need to manage files based on their content and context rather than just their location.

I gave my PC a search tool that reads inside every document, and Windows Search can't compete

Windows Search kept missing the details, so I gave my PC a smarter way to dig through documents.

7
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, a fresh perspective is all you need

I didn't expect to spend this much time exploring a file manager, but TagSpaces turned out to be a pleasant surprise. It doesn't try to imitate the tools Windows users already have, and that's what makes it stand out. I wouldn't recommend replacing your regular file manager with it, but I'd suggest giving it a try if you're curious about a more flexible way to handle files. It's one of those applications I'm happy to keep installed even after finishing this review.

TagSpaces

TagSpace is a powerful, file-based workspace that requires no cloud access for use. Productivity users can take advantage of it to manage files, tags, notes, maps, tasks, and kanban boards in one place.

item.title: Running two GPUs in one PC is back, but this time, games have nothing to do with it
item.itunes:title: Running two GPUs in one PC is back, but this time, games have nothing to do with it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you're too young to remember, there was a time when running a dual-GPU gaming setup was all the craze. Gamers who could afford it used to connect two and even three GPUs to reach performance heights mere single-GPU owners could only dream of. That may or may not be hyperbole, but there was active development around multi-GPU gaming by Nvidia and AMD, until there wasn't. By the end of the 2010s, support for multi-GPU gaming was effectively gone.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In the last few years, though, running multiple GPUs is back in vogue due to the popularity of local AI. Running local LLMs scales effectively across two (or more) GPUs, supercharging context windows, if not raw token performance. Also, buying two cheaper GPUs with enough VRAM doesn't hit your wallet as much as a single pricier GPU would, making the whole exercise worthwhile.

While the setup comes with its own challenges, users who already have a decent GPU in their PC should seriously consider pairing it with a second affordable card instead of hunting for a used RTX 5090.

Gaming used to be the reason behind dual-GPU setups

It hasn't been that way for a while

Nvidia's SLI and AMD's CrossFire garnered a cult following from the mid-2000s through the mid-2010s. This was a time when cutting-edge games were starting to require serious graphical power, especially if you wanted the best resolutions and framerates. Gamers who could afford multiple GPUs could effectively scale gaming performance in titles that were designed around the technology.

Not every game benefited from dual-GPU setups. Besides, microstutters and inconsistent driver support created quite a headache for gamers. As the 2010s were drawing to a close, these problems became too big to ignore, especially as the Pascal and Turing graphics cards had gotten powerful enough without the need for multi-GPU setups. Developers had stopped optimizing games for multiple GPUs, and the trend slowly died out.

Nvidia and AMD stopped supporting multi-GPU profiles around 2020-21. The RTX 3090 and 3090 Ti were the only 30 series cards to support SLI, and with the RTX 40 series, the support was fully gone. The industry shifted to single-GPU enhancements around AI, and multi-GPU gaming PCs became a dying breed.

Could multiple GPU gaming make a comeback?

It's unlikely, but there's a world where multiple GPU gaming makes a comeback thanks to modern APIs.

17
By  Adam Conway

Pairing your main GPU with a second card boosts local AI performance

Another reason behind poor GPU availability for gaming

Around March 2023, local AI enthusiasts revived the dual-GPU trend, but not for gaming this time. The rise of open-weight LLMs and tools like llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio made it possible to pool the resources of two graphics cards where a single one fell short. VRAM became the currency of LLM performance, and users started to see GPUs as professional tools instead of gaming-focused components.

While you don't get double the token performance by pairing two cards, you do get to fit significantly larger models. An RTX 5090 (if you can find one) has a massive 32GB framebuffer and the raw tensor performance to go with it. However, combining, say, two RTX 5060 Ti cards gives you the same amount of memory. Your investment is slashed by a huge margin, and your local AI math changes completely, even if the performance doesn't scale as you'd hope.

Pairing identical GPUs is recommended to avoid speed bottlenecks due to mismatched memory bandwidth and parallelism limits due to differing core counts. You can still use tensor splitting to carefully split model layers in a way that the card with less VRAM doesn't run out of memory.

Another thing you need to look out for is PCIe bifurcation on your motherboard. Many boards will limit the second GPU to x4 lanes wired to the chipset, limiting the performance. Higher-tier motherboards that provide 8 CPU-wired lanes each for both GPUs are recommended for dual-GPU setups.

I paired two cheap 16GB GPUs instead of buying one expensive 24GB card, and the math completely changed how I run local models

Sometimes cheaper wins

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Your two GPUs don't need to be identical

Or even current-gen models

Splitting your LLMs across two identical GPUs improves your context windows and allows you to leverage larger models, but not everyone needs to do it this way. Even if you have, say, a modern RTX GPU in your gaming PC and an older GTX card lying around, you can assign different tasks to each card. For instance, using an RTX 3080 Ti and a GTX 1080 together to run local image generation on the former and round-the-clock LLMs on the latter is a perfectly viable setup.

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models certainly help fit larger models on GPUs with around 12GB (or even 8GB) VRAM, allowing users to stretch the definition of what's possible on a mainstream local machine.

Even if you cannot buy two identical current-gen graphics cards, which most people can't in this market, a used older-gen GPU can still support your modern card by splitting the work. It won't be as high-end, but it'll still make great use of a dual-GPU setup.

Dual-GPU setups need to be financially viable

While it's technically possible to use multiple GPUs in a PC to split LLM layers or otherwise share local AI workload, you also need to make the project make sense financially. The initial investment is just a part of it; long-term power consumption needs to stay feasible compared to running a single GPU. Even the PSU requirements and thermal challenges of running two GPUs in a tower need to be considered before you dive in.

item.title: I stopped babysitting Claude Code, and now it gets work done while I'm away
item.itunes:title: I stopped babysitting Claude Code, and now it gets work done while I'm away
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You've likely seen the memes about developers walking around with their laptops open, so their AI coding agents can continue doing their thing. As funny as those memes are, I sort of hate to admit that I've been guilty of doing exactly that on multiple occasions.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For something that's supposed to save me time, I used to spend a surprising amount of time organizing my day around Claude Code. I'd either sit around waiting for it to finish a task or put off working on my projects altogether until I knew I'd have a couple of uninterrupted hours at my laptop.

What's ironic is that Claude Code has a few features specifically designed to eliminate the need to do either of those things. Since I started taking advantage of them, some of my most productive coding sessions have been ones I wasn't even around for.

Claude Code on the web is underrated

No laptop? No problem

For the longest time, pretty much all my Claude Code sessions took place within the terminal. I'd always been under the impression that Claude Code's web interface was primarily designed for people who weren't particularly comfortable working with a command-line interface. So, given how comfortable I'd gotten with the CLI, I never really saw a reason to turn toward it too much.

That changed when I was traveling recently. Not only did I not have access to a reliable internet connection at all times, but keeping my laptop switched on for extended periods wasn't practical either. That's when I remembered that Claude Code on the web was a thing, and I quickly realized I'd fundamentally misunderstood what made it so useful.

Unlike a traditional Claude Code session, where commands are executed and files are edited on your computer, Claude Code on the web does all of that within an isolated virtual machine (VM) hosted on Anthropic's infrastructure. Once I give Claude a task, I can shut my laptop down, lose access to the internet, and go about my day without interrupting its work. Another perk of offloading all of that work to a cloud VM is that I'm not consuming my laptop's resources every time Claude needs to install dependencies, run tests, or build a project.

While you don't necessarily need to connect Claude Code on the web to your GitHub account to use it, doing so makes it considerably more useful. I can give Claude access to my existing projects, have it implement features or fix bugs while I'm away, and have it push its changes to GitHub and even open a pull request once it's done.

Claude Code on the web also makes working on multiple tasks in parallel really easy. Since each cloud session runs within its own isolated environment, I don't have to worry about multiple instances of Claude stepping on each other's toes. I can queue up a bunch of unrelated tasks before heading out and come back to review all the work Claude's done while I was away.

I can take my local Claude Code sessions with me, too

A long-distance relationship with my terminal

One of my biggest frustrations with leaving Claude Code to work on something while I'm away has always been returning to my laptop an hour later, only to realize that Claude spent practically the entire hour waiting for me to approve a permission request.

That's where another ridiculously useful Claude Code feature called Remote Control comes in. By simply running the /remote-control command within an existing Claude Code session, I can make that very session accessible through the Claude app on my phone or even through a browser on another device. Claude retains access to everything it had access to before, and I can send follow-up prompts, approve permission requests, and monitor its progress without being anywhere near my laptop.

Unlike Claude Code on the web, Remote Control doesn't offload any of the actual work to the cloud. Everything still runs on my MacBook and, consequently, consumes its resources, and I also need to make sure my MacBook stays awake and connected to the internet.

However, since Claude Code can send me push notifications whenever it needs my input or finishes a task, I don't even need to actively monitor my sessions from my phone. And if Claude finishes what I initially asked it to do, I can give it something else to work on, regardless of where I am.

Some of my Claude Code sessions start without me

Clocking in while I'm clocked out

While being able to give Claude Code work to do while I'm away is convenient, there are also quite a few instances where I'm giving it practically the same instructions over and over again. If there's one thing I've learned from experimenting with AI automation, it's that I probably shouldn't be spending time initiating tasks that are predictable enough to automate.

One of my favorite automations, for instance, is a scheduled task I've set up through the Claude desktop app that cleans up my messy Downloads folder at the end of every week. Rather than having to remember to ask Claude to organize my files, identify duplicates, and get rid of unnecessary clutter, I've set it up to do so automatically.

Claude Code's cloud scheduled tasks (previously called Routines) take this concept a step further. I can give Claude a set of instructions, specify the repositories and connectors it needs access to, and decide when I want it to execute those instructions. Unlike my Downloads folder automation, which requires access to my MacBook, these tasks run in the cloud, meaning I don't even need to have my laptop switched on.

Claude Code is powerful, but this one setting made it far more useful for real projects

First thing you should change in Claude Code.

By  Parth Shah

For instance, I can have Claude Code audit one of my project's dependencies every Sunday and open a pull request with any necessary updates. These tasks don't necessarily need to run on a fixed schedule. I can have them triggered by specific GitHub events or even through an API call from an entirely different app.

For tasks that are a little more short-term, there's also Claude Code's /loop command. If I've asked Claude Code to open a pull request, for instance, I can have it check for new review comments or failing CI checks every ten minutes, rather than having to return to the session and explicitly ask it to do so.

At this point, not only do I not need to be around while Claude Code is working, but there are quite a few instances where I don't even need to be around to initiate the work in the first place! As impressive as the improvements to AI coding agents themselves have been over the past year, I'd argue that changing the way I work with them has made just as big a difference to my productivity.

That changed when I was traveling recently. Not only did I not have access to a reliable internet connection at all times, but keeping my laptop switched on for extended periods wasn't practical either. That's when I remembered that Claude Code on the web was a thing, and I quickly realized I'd fundamentally misunderstood what made it so useful.

Unlike a traditional Claude Code session, where commands are executed and files are edited on your computer, Claude Code on the web does all of that within an isolated virtual machine (VM) hosted on Anthropic's infrastructure. Once I give Claude a task, I can shut my laptop down, lose access to the internet, and go about my day without interrupting its work. Another perk of offloading all of that work to a cloud VM is that I'm not consuming my laptop's resources every time Claude needs to install dependencies, run tests, or build a project.

Rather than having to remember to ask Claude to organize my files, identify duplicates, and get rid of unnecessary clutter, I've set it up to do so automatically.

Claude Code's cloud scheduled tasks (previously called Routines) take this concept a step further. I can give Claude a set of instructions, specify the repositories and connectors it needs access to, and decide when I want it to execute those instructions. Unlike my Downloads folder automation, which requires access to my MacBook, these tasks run in the cloud, meaning I don't even need to have my laptop switched on.

Claude Code is powerful, but this one setting made it far more useful for real projects

For instance, I can have Claude Code audit one of my project's dependencies every Sunday and open a pull request with any necessary updates. These tasks don't necessarily need to run on a fixed schedule. I can have them triggered by specific GitHub events or even through an API call from an entirely different app.

For tasks that are a little more short-term, there's also Claude Code's /loop command. If I've asked Claude Code to open a pull request, for instance, I can have it check for new review comments or failing CI checks every ten minutes, rather than having to return to the session and explicitly ask it to do so.

At this point, not only do I not need to be around while Claude Code is working, but there are quite a few instances where I don't even need to be around to initiate the work in the first place! As impressive as the improvements to AI coding agents themselves have been over the past year, I'd argue that changing the way I work with them has made just as big a difference to my productivity.
